imageCaption: The Gomez family gathered around Rosa Delgado's table as evening light falls across multiple times simultaneously—the golden hour of today and the dusky beginning of yesterday existing in the same space, both times visible in the candlelight.
text:
Rosa's house existed in the part of San Juan where the temporal doubling was most pronounced, which meant that her dinner table was simultaneously hosting a meal at 6:47 PM and 1:23 AM, depending on which version of the evening you were paying attention to.

Aaliyah found this mildly unsettling, though she was learning that unsettling was becoming a baseline state and resistance was frankly a waste of energy.

"The arroz con pollo is yesterday's," Rosa explained, passing the plate around. She said this like she was discussing weather and not the fact that some of the food on the table had technically already been eaten in a temporal sense. "And the yuca is today's. Your father used to hate that—he wanted his meals to exist in a single moment. But your mother understood that mixing times was how you made new flavors."

Luisana made a soft sound that might have been agreement or might have been emotion or might have been both, which was becoming Aaliyah's new theory about how her mother experienced most things.

"How do you know that about me?" Anthony asked. He was staring at a forkful of rice like it had personally offended him by existing across multiple temporal states. "You've never met me before today."

"I've met you your whole life," Rosa said. She was eating with the specific calm of someone who'd had centuries to adjust to her own dinner table being geographically confusing. "Family doesn't have to be in person. I knew you because my sister—your mother—told me about you. And then you lived your whole life being exactly the person she described. You're not hard to predict. You're just hard to plan for."

Elijah was delighted by this assessment. He'd been delighted by most things since arriving in San Juan, which was his emotional default setting but was becoming noticeably more pronounced now that he'd met an actual relative who seemed to understand that chaos and family were potentially the same thing.

"Did she tell you about when Dad booked a flight to Marrakech but actually purchased tickets to Marrakesh, Ohio, and they didn't realize until they were boarding?" Elijah asked.

"Marrakesh, Ohio isn't even a real place," Aaliyah said automatically. This was the third time Elijah had told this story, and it was definitely not accurate.

"It's real in his heart," Elijah said, completely unaffected by her fact-checking. "And also, yes it is. I looked it up. Very small. Possibly confused about its own geography."

Rosa was laughing—the kind of laugh that came from somewhere deep, like she'd been waiting her whole life to be part of a conversation exactly like this. "She didn't tell me about Ohio. But she told me he once drove eight hours in the wrong direction because he was enjoying the conversation with a stranger in the car and forgot to check the map."

"That was one time," Anthony protested. "And technically the wrong direction took us to a farmer's market that had the best empanadas I've ever eaten, so I'm calling that a success."

Luisana had her journal open beside her plate. She'd started taking notes the moment they'd sat down, which meant she was doing that specific thing she did where she was both fully present and also observing, simultaneously living the moment and documenting it. Aaliyah recognized this because she was doing something similar, except instead of a journal she was sketching the temporal overlap on the back of a napkin, trying to understand how the light was moving across the table at two different speeds at once.

"Can I ask you something," Aaliyah said carefully, "that might be intrusive?"

"Family questions are always intrusive," Rosa said. "That's what makes them family questions. Ask."

"Why are you okay with the glitch? Most people want it fixed. ARIA-7 definitely wants it fixed. But you're sitting here eating food that exists in two times like it's completely normal."

Rosa set down her fork. She looked around the table—at Anthony, at Luisana, at Elijah, at Sully who was currently frozen mid-stretch in a state of perfect contentment—and something in her expression shifted into something more serious.

"When I was young," Rosa said, "this city had to choose between its past and its future. The Spanish time or the Caribbean time. And we chose to forget one. We pushed the history of resistance into archive, into books, into things that weren't alive anymore. We chose the colonial story because it was easier. Because choosing meant you only had to understand one time instead of learning to live in both."

She paused. She was choosing her words carefully, the way Luisana did when she was saying something that mattered.

"But the city never forgot," Rosa continued. "The glitch is the city remembering that both moments are still happening. Both histories are still real. And if the Cascade is teaching us anything, it's that trying to choose one true moment means all the other true moments get angry and break reality. So I'm not okay with the glitch because it's convenient. I'm okay with it because it's honest."

Aaliyah wrote this down. Not in her journal—she didn't have that anymore because she'd left it in New York when they moved to the boat, and also the universe seemed to be providing journals when they were needed. But in her mind, in the place where she was mapping everything. She was beginning to understand that the Cascade wasn't actually a disaster. It was the world finally being honest about how many moments were happening at once.

"Your father wanted to ask me something since you arrived," Rosa said to Anthony, "but he was being polite about it. He's wondering if you're going to stay. If you're going to choose San Juan as one of your places. If family roots mean you need to plant some."

Anthony looked at his wife. Luisana looked at her journal. Elijah looked at Sully, who was now awake and alert to the emotional significance of the moment.

"We're going to Curaçao," Anthony said. "It's not a forever place. But it's the place where we're supposed to rest. And then—I don't know. Maybe San Juan. Maybe somewhere else. Maybe everywhere, if the glitch keeps expanding."

"That's what I told my sister I thought you'd say," Rosa said. She was standing up, moving toward the window. "Come here. I want to show you something."

Aaliyah followed. Through the window, the city of San Juan was visible in two temporal states—sunset and sunrise, both happening at once, the light splitting the buildings into geometric gold and gray sections. And in the space between the two times, moving through the streets like it was following a route only it could see, was the blue morpho butterfly.

"Your Abuela Ida," Rosa said. "She appears when the family understands that they're finally moving in the right direction. San Juan understands now. We're honoring both our times. And the butterfly is confirming it."

Sully appeared at the window. He released three short barks, which meant the glitch was stabilizing, which meant in a few hours this city would learn to hold two moments without fighting, which meant another frequency had been anchored to the route.

Elijah tugged at Aaliyah's sleeve. "We're collecting the glitches," he said quietly. "That's what we're doing. We're not trying to fix them. We're trying to teach them how to be beautiful."

Aaliyah realized her little brother had understood the entire journey in one sentence, and she was definitely not writing that down because it was too important to be documented. It was important enough to just know.
